# Isaiah 55: Research notes, verse by verse

**What these notes cover:** I found good verse-by-verse material from the older commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes, Poole, Calvin, Matthew Henry, Wesley/Benson) and from Guzik (Enduring Word), Got Questions, Desiring God and Bible.org. I found **nothing** from the Catholic or Orthodox sites, Bible Odyssey, the Lutheran sites, or the Pentecostal sites other than Guzik. I also found no material on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings. Those sections are left out. The Enduring Word page was cut off partway through vv. 10–11, so I have nothing from Guzik on vv. 12–13. For the two pages I read in full (Enduring Word and Wesley's Notes) I give the URL without a quote reference.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott says the water, wine and milk all stand for spiritual blessings. The whole context shows that the water, the wine, the milk are all, symbols of spiritual blessings. He also links the invitation to the grieving woman of Isaiah 54. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-1.htm
- Poole: "buy" means receiving what is offered free. Nor can this be understood of buying properly, because here is no price paid. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-1.htm
- The Cambridge Bible note says the Hebrew word for "buy" is used only of buying grain. It also says the picture probably recalls God's miracle fountain for his people (Isa 41:18), rather than street water-sellers calling out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-1.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word): the invitation is for everyone who is thirsty, and only the thirsty will come. He takes "waters… wine… milk" to mean that growing in the Christian life is as free as entering it, and he quotes Spurgeon on God stooping to cry "Ho!" He suggests Jesus may have had this passage in mind in John 7:37. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/
- **Where interpreters differ (what the waters are):** Calvin, from the Reformed side, rejects two common readings. Some view the word "waters" as referring to the doctrine of the Gospel, and others to the Holy Spirit; but neither of these expositions, in my opinion, is correct. He stresses that the invitation is general and goes to everyone without distinction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/55.htm
  - Poole, by contrast, takes the waters as the graces and comforts of God's Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-1.htm
  - Matthew Henry adds a sacramental note. He urges readers to come to holy ordinances, which may look plain but to believers are like wine and milk. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_055.cfm
  - Wesley (Methodist) takes the wine and milk as all gospel blessings, especially "peace and joy in the Holy Ghost" and the love of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: "spend money" is literally "weigh silver," because money was weighed before coins existed. The affections of the great mass of the Israelites were set on worldly things. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-2.htm
- Ellicott: Israel is called to accept the true bread for "not-money," meaning the simple "hearing of faith." He reads "fatness" as overflowing spiritual joy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-2.htm
- Gill applies "that which is not bread" to false teaching, which he calls chaff rather than food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-2.htm
- Guzik draws three duties from the verse: listen carefully, choose what is good, and let your soul enjoy it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/
- **Older critical view:** Keil and Delitzsch report that Hitzig and Knobel understand by water, wine, and milk, the rich material blessings which awaited the exiles on their return. That is a material reading, not a spiritual one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Barnes: God binds himself in covenant with all who would come to him. It would not be with the nation of the Jews, as such, or with any community, as such. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-3.htm
- Cambridge: the comparison means the two are the same thing, not just equally certain. The covenant's contents are the mercies promised to David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-3.htm
- Pulpit: Isaiah has already taught that people, and Israel especially, broke the earlier "everlasting covenant" (Isa 24:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/isaiah-55.html
- The Bible Hub summary calls "sure mercies of David" a messianic reference, ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ. Precept Austin lists the verse as quoted in Acts 13:34 about the Messiah's resurrection. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/55.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_commentaries
- The Biblical Illustrator points out that the Hebrew says "cut a covenant," recalling sacrifices cut in two when covenants were made. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tbi/isaiah-55.html
- **Where traditions differ (can people respond on their own?):**
  - Gill (Particular Baptist, i.e. Calvinist): There must be life before hearing; men must be made alive before they can come to Christ spiritually. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-3.htm
  - Wesley (Methodist): the covenant is the one made with Abraham and then David, whose chief blessing was Christ dying for sins. Here "David" stands for the Son of David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
  - Guzik focuses on God's sure, unfailing mercy shown to David himself, the sinner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/

**v. 4**
- **Where traditions differ (who "him" is):**
  - Wesley: "him" is the David just mentioned, "even Christ." Christ is a witness to all people who declares God's will and confirms his promises, including the calling of the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
  - Gill notes the verse is confessedly understood of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-3.htm
  - Matthew Henry: Christ is given to be *a leader.* We know not what to do that we may be qualified or it, and become sharers in it, but he is given for *a commander,* to show us what to do and enable us to do it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_055.cfm
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel, premillennial) takes it of David as God's model leader, a witness *to* the people and a leader *for* them. He says it is fulfilled spiritually in David-like leaders, and finally when the literal, resurrected King David rules Israel in the millennium (citing Jer 30:9 and Ezek 34, 37). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/
  - Precept Austin warns that some commentaries have "replaced" Israel with the Church. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_commentaries

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: The object of address in this verse appears to be the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-5.htm
- Wesley agrees ("Thou, O Messiah"). He says the "glory" is God confirming Christ's word by miracles, and especially by his resurrection and ascension. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
- Gill applies the verse to the spread of the gospel through the apostles and later missions. He also says the elect, though known to God beforehand, are "unknown" until they are called. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-5.htm
- Cambridge takes "thou" to be Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-5.htm
- Guzik thinks it may mean both Israel and David, with final fulfilment when the nations stream to Israel in the millennium. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/

**v. 6**
- Keil and Delitzsch: Israel should press into fellowship with God now, now that He approaches Israel, and offers it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-6.htm
- Barnes: God is in one sense near at all times, but some times are more favourable than others, such as preaching, illness or revival. If those times pass unused, a time comes when it is too late. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-6.htm
- Gill quotes the Targum ("while ye are alive"). He also offers a "place" reading: seek God where he may be found, in his house and ordinances. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-6.htm
- **Where traditions differ:**
  - Wesley and Benson (Methodist): "while" means In this day of grace, while he offers mercy and reconciliation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm . Benson calls the call general, for Jews and Gentiles alike. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-6.htm . Wesley preached his last sermon on this text. https://bible.org/illustration/wesley%E2%80%99s-last-sermon
  - Guzik adds a note on grace: God can be found when our hearts are inclined to look for him, and that inclination is itself God's gift. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/
  - Piper (Desiring God, Reformed Baptist): seeking the Lord means calling on him, that is, praying. You can't seek him where he is not found — in sin. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-great-invitation-a-high-way-for-low-sinners
- **Modern scholarship (NET notes):** the NET translates "while he makes himself available." Its note says Heb "while he allows himself to be found." The Niphal form has a tolerative force here. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Isa&chapter=55&verse=6

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: God's will is to "multiply pardon," if man will only turn to him. It traces the promise back to 2 Chronicles 7:14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-7.htm
- Guzik: repentance means turning from our way to God's. "Thoughts" shows the battle often happens in the mind (2 Cor 10:5; Rom 12:2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/
- **Where traditions differ (what repentance includes):**
  - Gill (Calvinist Baptist): the "thoughts" to give up include especially his thoughts of being justified by his own righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-7.htm
  - Wesley: "Return – by sincere repentance, and faith." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
  - Benson (Methodist) presses for a changed life. Returning means sincere repentance and faith, productive of new obedience. Outward seeking does no lasting good without a reformed life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-6.htm

**v. 8**
- Barnes: the verse refers primarily to the subject of pardon, though it is true of God's ways in general. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-8.htm
- Wesley: people are slow to forgive, but God is ready to forgive every penitent, however great their sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
- Pulpit links it to the return from Babylon: people can hardly imagine the deliverance God plans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-8.htm
- A sermon quoted on the same Bible Hub page sees the root of sin in "your thoughts… your ways," that is, self-reliance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Gill: the gap between earth and sky shows how heavenly, eternal and unsearchable God's ways are. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-9.htm
- Guzik: we can relate to God's thoughts but cannot master them. The distance is meant to keep us humble, not to put us off seeking him (quoting Spurgeon). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-55/

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: The rain and the snow are God's ministers (Psalm 148:8), and go forth from him, just as his word does. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-10.htm
- Calvin points to two results of rain: food now, and seed for next year's crop. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/55.htm
- Got Questions explains the picture of rain and snow that do not go back up without doing their work. https://www.gotquestions.org/not-return-void.html

**v. 11**
- Poole: the picture is an allusion to an ambassador who returns without despatching that business for which he was sent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-11.htm
- Delitzsch, quoted in the Pulpit Commentary, says God's word runs like a swift messenger and does not come back until the Sender's will is done. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-11.htm
- Pulpit: the "word" meant here is especially the promise of deliverance from Babylon. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/55-11.htm
- **Modern translation:** the NET renders it the promise that I make does not return to me, having accomplished nothing. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/55-11.htm
- **Where traditions differ (God's word and unbelief):**
  - Calvin (Reformed) says God's promises bear fruit, provided that we do not prevent it by our unbelief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/55.htm
  - Gill offers a Christ-centred reading: the word may be Christ himself, who went back to heaven "not empty" but with a harvest of souls. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/isaiah/55-11.html
  - Wesley limits it to God's promises to pardon even the greatest sinners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
  - Barnes says even a rejected gospel leaves people without excuse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-11.htm
- **Popular use, and a caution:**
  - Got Questions warns that the promise is that God's Word will accomplish what He wants it to, not necessarily what we want it to. https://www.gotquestions.org/not-return-void.html
  - A Bible Hub Q&A uses the verse to encourage Scripture-based prayers. https://www.biblehub.com/q/what_does_'word_won't_return_void'_mean.htm
  - Chuck Smith tells readers to start using the Word and quit defending it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/55-11.html

**v. 12**
- Gill: the verse may literally mean the Jews' joyful return from captivity, but it can be applied spiritually to conversion, with the return from Babylon as a type. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-12.htm
- Pulpit: A strong contrast is frequently drawn between the exodus from Babylon and that from Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-12.htm
- Poole and Wesley say even unthinking creation will seem to rejoice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
- Bible Hub's summary links the verse to Psalm 98:7–8 and Romans 8:19–21. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/55.htm

**v. 13**
- Barnes: under the gospel the change would be as great in the moral world as if a field all overrun with briers should at once become thick set with myrtles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-13.htm
- Wesley: "the church shall be delivered from pernicious things." The change will be a lasting monument to God's power and faithfulness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/55.htm
- Bible Hub's summary: Thorn to cypress reversal points back to Genesis 3:18 curses undone. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/55.htm
- **More literal views:**
  - Cambridge (citing Dillmann) thinks the desert growth stays as a real monument, not to be regarded as a mere poetical figure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/55-13.htm
  - MacArthur (quoted on Precept Austin) says God is bound to bring Israel back and bless it, citing Isaiah 55:10–12. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_commentaries

**Whole chapter (modern scholarship):** Bible.org reports that Clifford reads the chapter as one poem in three parts (vv. 1–5, 6–11, 12–13), summoning the exiles to end their separation from Yahweh's presence by leaving Babylon and coming to Zion. https://bible.org/seriespage/21-god-s-exhortation-receive-his-grace-isaiah-551-13
